title: Ignorance of scripture
hookLine: Jerome: not knowing the scriptures is not knowing Christ (CCC 133)

cards: Count the open books this week. Augustine in a garden, hearing take and read, and opening Paul. Augustine and Monica at a window, talking about a life no eye has seen, words Paul quotes.
Late have I loved thee, his story turned into prayer. The City of God, sending pilgrims to Jeremiah's advice. Love, then do, preached on First John.
And Jerome, giving the book a common tongue. Again and again, the page is close at hand. Jerome says why, in one sentence the Catechism still quotes.

teach.b: First, the sentence. Jerome wrote it at the start of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah. In his Latin: ignoratio Scripturarum ignoratio Christi est.
Ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it in its section on scripture, and so did the Second Vatican Council. Second, how he gets there.
It isn't a slogan; it's an argument in two steps. Jesus told his hearers to search the scriptures, because they bear witness to him. And Paul calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

teach.h: SEARCH THE SCRIPTURES; CHRIST IS WISDOM.
teach.b: So, Jerome reasons, if you don't know the scriptures, you don't know God's power and God's wisdom, and that means you don't know Christ. Third, why put this line at the front of a book on Isaiah, an ancient prophet?
Jerome says Isaiah speaks so clearly of Christ that he reads less like a prophet than a gospel writer. Fourth, what this asks of an ordinary reader. Not a degree.
Jerome wrote this commentary at the request of a woman who studied scripture with him, not for a faculty. Some readers put it this way: knowing scripture is like knowing a friend.
You learn the voice by listening often.
You can know a lot about someone and still not know them. Read like that, the line is less a scolding than an invitation: for Jerome, time with the book is time with Christ.

how: The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes Jerome's line when it urges the faithful to read scripture often, and some Catholics keep a daily habit of reading the day's Mass readings.

games.q: you're Jerome, starting a commentary on Isaiah. how do you open?
o: with a list of grammar rules.
with why knowing scripture means knowing Christ.

games.why: he opens with his reason: search the scriptures, Christ is God's wisdom, so ignorance of scripture is ignorance of Christ.

practice: Open a Bible, or a Bible app, to any of the four Gospels; Mark is short, if you want somewhere to start.
Read one page slowly, without trying to study it, just listening for the voice: what Jesus says, what he does, who he's talking to.
Then go back to one line that caught you and stay with it, and if you pray, ask to know him through what you've read.

wordCard.voice: Jerome. The scholar who wrote that ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ, in his prologue to the prophet Isaiah. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ — from Jerome's prologue to Isaiah.

carryVoice: Your line: know the book, know him. One page at a time is enough. See you tomorrow.
